components.text: Whether the seven accepted letters themselves lack an unambiguous earthly ministry or terrestrial death location.
Whether restricting the evidentiary corpus to seven letters is methodologically justified.
Challenges the restriction of relevant Pauline evidence to seven accepted letters.
Must positively warrant treating all thirteen letters as Pauline.
Whether Pauline letters contain meaningful biographical particulars bearing on an earthly Jesus.
Whether mortal embodiment and the cited biographical markers are compatible with a wholly nonterrestrial saving career.
Whether every cited marker comes from the securely accepted seven-letter corpus.
Supplies Pauline references offered as counterexamples to alleged terrestrial silence.
Must show that these markers favor an earthly setting over a flesh-bearing celestial interpretation.
Whether the rulers who crucified Jesus provide a secure human and terrestrial biographical marker.
Whether expanding the Pauline corpus resolves the identity of the rulers in First Corinthians.
Reinterprets the cited crucifying rulers as demonic powers whose ignorance explains the concealed plan.
Challenges the broader corpus claim.
Whether crucifixion terminology necessarily locates the event on Earth among ordinary human practices.
Explains how crucifixion language could remain intelligible in a celestial setting.
Addresses Pauline corpus scope.
Whether First Corinthians identifies the crucifying rulers as demonic rather than human authorities.
Whether a heavenly-copy cosmology overrides the local human-wisdom contrast in First Corinthians.
Uses the immediate Corinthian contrast with human wisdom to identify the rulers as human.
Challenges the broader heavenly-crucifixion cosmology.
Whether demonic participation requires construing the named rulers as exclusively spiritual agents.
Whether spiritual participation requires relocating the crucifixion itself to a heavenly realm.
Argues that human rulers are the contextual referents even if spiritual forces participated.
Directly locates the crucifixion on Earth rather than in a heavenly counterpart.
Whether references to James and brothers of the Lord provide unambiguous biological particularity.
Offers a cultic reading of the cited brother references.
Addresses the rulers interpretation.
Whether the brother terminology is better explained as cultic membership than biological kinship.
Whether familial references provide historical particularity for an earthly Jesus.
Argues that James and other brothers are biological relatives using convergent Pauline and later narrative references.
Uses the sibling references as broader terrestrial evidence.
Whether later Gospel and Acts family traditions can determine the meaning of Paul's earlier ambiguous terminology.
Whether First Corinthians 9 independently requires biological brothers.
Separates Paul's ambiguous language from later Gospel and Acts family traditions.
Challenges use of brother references as Pauline terrestrial markers.
Whether Acts's narrative is so freely fictionalized that substantial historical accuracy cannot be recovered.
Whether Acts possesses sufficient independence to corroborate Pauline-era historical claims.
Offers an undesigned correspondence between Acts and Paul's letters as evidence against pervasive fabrication.
Establishes Acts' independence from Paul or the Gospel family tradition.
Whether selected correspondences establish Acts's broad reliability or authorship by Paul's companion.
Whether Acts contradicts Paul's own chronology concerning Judea and Arabia.
Counters correspondence-based reliability with specific chronology and mission contradictions.
Challenges Acts' family evidence specifically.
Whether Acts's many-days wording can accommodate Paul's Arabian interval rather than contradict it.
Whether cumulative internal and external details are expected under wholesale literary fabrication.
Whether Acts contradicts Paul's Judean fame and Gentile-mission claims beyond the Arabian chronology.
Explains the Arabian interval through narrative telescoping within “many days.”
Uses cumulative internal and external fit against wholesale fabrication.
Whether detailed narrative correspondences are more expected from historical information than broad literary fabrication.
Whether later Gospel narratives possess enough independence to corroborate historical information.
Answers the earlier Acts contradictions or their implications for later-source reliability.
Challenges literary fabrication generally through Gospel examples.
Whether apparent interlocking details require independent historical information rather than literary dependence.
Explains apparent coincidences through John's literary use and rewriting of Synoptic sources.
Extends the dependence explanation to Acts-Paul correspondences.
Whether deliberate harmonization plausibly explains why the relevant feeding details remain dispersed across distant passages.
Whether the sources' independence is established generally beyond this particular dispersed pattern.
Argues that the relevant facts are too dispersed across chapters and Gospels to look like explicit harmonization.
Addresses later-source contradiction evidence outside the Gospels.
Whether dispersed character and location details are difficult to produce through conscious use of earlier Gospel sources.
Whether the broader set of alleged undesigned coincidences can all be explained by the same selection mechanism.
Explains selection of Philip from source material without requiring restatement of every location detail.
Provides a general literary mechanism for the broader coincidence argument.
